content: 1. Among the 1,914 subjects who received cefuroxime in 24 clinical studies, 901 (47%) were aged 65 years or older, and 421 (22%) were aged 75 years or older. 2. No significant differences in safety or effectiveness were observed between elderly subjects and younger subjects. Additionally, other reported clinical experiences have not identified differences in responses between these age groups. However, the possibility of increased susceptibility to drug effects in some older individuals cannot be excluded. 3. This drug is primarily excreted by the kidneys, and patients with impaired renal function may be at a higher risk of toxic reactions. 4. Since elderly patients are more likely to have reduced renal function, careful dose selection is recommended, and monitoring of renal function may be beneficial. 5. There is no FDA guidance on the use of cefuroxime sodium (injection) with respect to specific gender populations. 6. There is no FDA guidance on the use of cefuroxime sodium (injection) with respect to specific racial populations. 7. There is no FDA guidance on the use of cefuroxime sodium (injection) in patients with renal impairment. 8. There is no FDA guidance on the use of cefuroxime sodium (injection) in patients with hepatic impairment. 9. There is no FDA guidance on the use of cefuroxime sodium (injection) in women of reproductive potential or in males. 10. There is no FDA guidance on the use of cefuroxime sodium (injection) in immunocompromised patients. 11. Cefuroxime sodium can be administered via intramuscular or intravenous routes. 12. Cephalosporins, including cefuroxime, may be associated with a reduction in prothrombin activity. 13. Patients at risk for reduced prothrombin activity include those with renal or hepatic impairment, poor nutritional status, those receiving prolonged antimicrobial therapy, and those previously stabilized on anticoagulant therapy. 14. Prothrombin time should be monitored in at-risk patients, and exogenous Vitamin K should be administered as indicated. 15. When cefuroxime injection solutions are prepared as directed with sterile water for injection, they maintain satisfactory potency for 24 hours at room temperature and for 48 hours under refrigeration (5°C). 16. These solutions can be further diluted to concentrations between 1 and 30 mg/mL in various compatible solutions, retaining no more than a 10% loss of activity for 24 hours at room temperature or at least 7 days under refrigeration. 17. Unused solutions should be discarded after the specified time periods. 18. Cefuroxime injection solutions are compatible for 24 hours at room temperature when admixed in IV infusion with heparin (10 and 50 U/mL) in 0.9% sodium chloride injection and potassium chloride (10 and 40 mEq/L) in 0.9% sodium chloride injection. 19. Sodium bicarbonate injection is not recommended for diluting cefuroxime injection. 20. Frozen solutions of cefuroxime are stable for 6 months when stored at -20°C. 21. Frozen solutions should be thawed at room temperature and not refrozen. Thawing by immersion in water baths or microwave irradiation is not recommended. 22. Thawed solutions may be stored for up to 24 hours at room temperature or for 7 days in a refrigerator. 23. Parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration whenever the solution and container permit. 24. Cefuroxime powder, solutions, and suspensions may darken depending on storage conditions, but this does not adversely affect product potency. 25. Overdosage of cephalosporins, including cefuroxime, can cause cerebral irritation leading to convulsions. 26. Serum levels of cefuroxime can be reduced by hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis. 27. Cefuroxime is a bactericidal agent that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis. 28. It is active in the presence of some beta-lactamases, including penicillinases and cephalosporinases, produced by Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. 29. Cefuroxime is a semisynthetic, broad-spectrum cephalosporin antibiotic for parenteral administration. 30. It is the sodium salt of (6R,7R)-3-carbamoyloxymethyl-7-ceph-3-em-4-carboxylate. 31. Cefuroxime exhibits in vitro activity against a wide range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms and is highly stable in the presence of beta-lactamases of certain Gram-negative bacteria. 32. The bactericidal action of cefuroxime results from inhibition of cell wall synthesis. 33. Cefuroxime is usually active against organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Streptococcus pyogenes (and other streptococci). 34. Most strains of enterococci, including Enterococcus faecalis, are resistant to cefuroxime. 35. Methicillin-resistant staphylococci and Listeria monocytogenes are resistant to cefuroxime. 36. Some strains of Morganella morganii, Enterobacter cloacae, and Citrobacter species have shown resistance to cefuroxime and other cephalosporins in in vitro tests. 37. Pseudomonas, Campylobacter, Legionella, Acinetobacter calcoaceticus, and most strains of Serratia species and Proteus vulgaris are resistant to most firstand second-generation cephalosporins.
